summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual activity is criminalised under section 377 of the penal code, a provision introduced in 1886. It prohibits carnal intercourse with any man, woman or animal and provides for imprisonment ranging between life and a term of not less than two years, extendable to ten years, with a fine of between 400 and 1,000 rupees. The prohibition applies regardless of consent or privacy, and it reaches heterosexual anal and oral sex as well. Enforcement has been described as inconsistent, but the provision remains in active use: in November 2018 the HIV-positive advocate Aung Myo Htut was charged under it in Yangon over an alleged offence against an employee.

Transgender people are additionally targeted under section 35(c) of the Police Act 1945, known locally as the shadow law or darkness law, which allows police to detain anyone they consider to be behaving suspiciously after sunset. A related provision on face covering carries up to three months' imprisonment and is used specifically against transgender people. Other provisions cited as available against LGBT people include sections 269 and 270 on negligently spreading a sexually transmitted disease, section 290 on public nuisance with fines up to 200 rupees, sections 292, 293 and 294 on obscene material, songs or public acts, section 372 on buying or selling a prostitute under eighteen, section 469 on a marriage ceremony absent a legal marriage, and section 5(j) of the Emergency Provisions Act on anything affecting morality negatively.

Myanmar does not recognise gender identity and does not permit transgender people to change the gender assigned to them at birth. No legal gender recognition procedure or documentary process is described in the sources. Transgender people are consequently subject to police harassment, sexual assault including rape, mistreatment and extortion.

Documented incidents include the 2013 arrest in Mandalay of transgender women who were forced to strip and paraded naked while being photographed, which police described as a public service, and the case of the transgender woman Nat Nat We, arrested, stripped and beaten in Yangon and held for 14 days after walking home at night, with police accusing her of sex work. Police violence against transgender women is routine.

Since the coup of 1 February 2021 the risk environment has worsened. Authorities have carried out attacks, arrests, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people, and torture and sexual violence in detention are documented. Militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life, and a June 2024 submission to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions identified killings of LGBTIQ+ people in military-controlled areas, naming intensified enforcement of section 377 as an aggravating factor.

The conscription law announced in February 2024 has driven queer people into fear and displacement. In 2025 the junta banned seven LGBTQ-themed books as obscene and announced prosecutions for their publishers. The October 2022 Organization Registration Law imposes prison terms on NGOs that fail to comply, constraining the civil-society organisations that provide community support.

Myanmar has no enforceable legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The measures that exist are symbolic or non-binding: the 2019 Child Rights Law contains a non-discrimination clause referencing sexual orientation but applies only to children and has no enforcement mechanism; the 2020 MRTV Broadcasting Guidelines discourage discriminatory media portrayals without legal penalties; and the 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights lists LGBTQ people as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery but is a planning document rather than law. A survey of LGBT respondents found that 50 per cent had no confidence in the legal system and more than 68 per cent feared repercussions from abusers.

Myanmar does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions. A 2014 unofficial wedding ceremony by a couple who had been together for ten years drew widespread attention and a backlash from social conservatives who questioned why the anti-homosexuality laws were not enforced against them. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be classified as same-sex under Myanmar law, there is no route to legal recognition.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion data points in a different direction from the legal regime. A 2020 poll found that 74 per cent agreed being LGBTQ should be legal, against 23 per cent who disagreed, and 81 per cent agreed that LGBT people deserve equality and equal treatment, against 12 per cent who disagreed. Activists have described a growing climate of societal acceptance and tolerance.

Social mores about sexuality have been described as extremely conservative, and in local Buddhist tradition those born LGBTQ are understood as facing punishment for sins committed in a past life. Historically, official homophobia, limited public awareness and a lack of community role models rendered LGBTQ people invisible in Burmese society.

Cultural visibility for transgender people is uneven. As nat kadaws, or spirit mediums, transgender people can be afforded respect and veneration otherwise denied to them, and occult is a local term for the transgender community. Mya Thet Mu, a gay woman from Myanmar, is documented as saying that lesbians are often seen as less acceptable than gay men and transgender people.
localsOnly:
Trans women are frequently denied equal access to many professions, which limits opportunities and pushes them towards a narrow set of occupations. Three options are described as respectable: beautician, fashion designer, or nat kadaw. Overrepresentation in spirit medium work and in sex work follows from that exclusion.

Access to healthcare is shaped by criminalisation and stigma. Section 377 was identified in 2013 by Aung San Suu Kyi as hampering the country's efforts to combat HIV, and gay men, especially those living with HIV or AIDS, are stigmatised. The 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights includes LGBTQ individuals as a vulnerable group in healthcare delivery, but it is a planning document rather than an enforceable law.

In June 2019 Kyaw Zin Win, a young gay man working as a librarian at Myanmar Imperial University in Yangon, died by suicide after continuous harassment and bullying from colleagues. More than 600 people attended his funeral and a rainbow flag was wrapped around his coffin. The university opened an investigation and suspended three staff members, and the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission launched a separate investigation and called for the enactment of anti-discrimination provisions.

Same-sex couples can cohabit freely in Yangon and Mandalay and can hold ceremonial marriages without legal persecution, but these ceremonies carry no legal standing.
outOfScopeNotes:
No legal gender recognition procedure or documentary process for transgender people is described in the available sources. Whether any administrative practice exists outside statute is not sourced.

Enforcement of section 377 is not systematically recorded. The provision has been described as not strictly enforced while remaining in active use, and no prosecution statistics are available to indicate how often it is applied.

The 2022 Gender Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights is a planning document with no enforcement mechanism, and the 2020 MRTV Broadcasting Guidelines carry no legal penalties. Neither creates a remedy for a visitor or resident who experiences discrimination.

How the 2024 conscription law's medical and documentation screening treats transgender people is not addressed in the sources.
